title: Service Correspondence (Letters, Memoranda, Emails)
source: Defence Forces Service Writing Manual 2024 (JP-04), Chapter 3
notes: Rules for the twelve types of Service correspondence. Formats are illustrated in Annexes A-F to Chapter 3.

rules.title: All correspondence must have a file reference, date and signature block
rules.description: All correspondences must have a file reference, date and signature block.

check.where: The letterhead area and end of the correspondence.

rules.title: Text should consist of an introduction, a body and a conclusion
rules.description: In all but the shortest letters on routine matters, the text should cover a single subject and consist of an introduction, a body and a conclusion.
rules.notes: These headings are seldom used in letter writing, so this is a structural heuristic.

rules.title: Letters to the public omit subject heading and paragraph numbers
rules.description: To help create a more personal tone when writing a letter to a person outside the MoD/KDF, leave out the subject heading and paragraph numbers.

rules.title: Abbreviations must not be used in letters to civilians
rules.description: In correspondence with civilian authorities or members of the public, abbreviations should not be used.

rules.title: Most Defence Forces correspondence is written in the third person
rules.description: Most correspondence is written in the third person, except formal letters, demi-official letters, letters from a commander conveying personal views, and letters from headquarters which may use the first person plural.
rules.notes: Heuristic: flag frequent first-person singular usage ('I', 'my') in non-formal/DO letters.

rules.title: Formal letters begin with the salutation 'Sir'
rules.description: A formal letter begins with the salutation 'Sir' and the text begins 'I have the honour to ...', except the Navy circumstantial letter which begins 'I regret to report ...'.

rules.title: Formal letters end 'I have the honour to be, Sir, Your obedient Servant'
rules.description: A formal letter always ends 'I have the honour to be, Sir, Your obedient Servant'.

params.pattern: I have the honour to be, Sir, Your obedient Servant

rules.title: Formal letters are signed by the originator
rules.description: A formal letter is addressed only to a senior or equal and is signed by the originator.

rules.title: DO letters are restricted to one subject
rules.description: Demi-Official (DO) letters permit an informal approach but must be restricted to one subject and filed in the normal way.
rules.notes: Human review: a DO letter must be restricted to one subject.

rules.title: DO letters use 'Dear ...' salutation and 'Yours' ending in manuscript
rules.description: The salutation 'Dear ........' and the ending 'Yours.' are inserted in manuscript by the originator.

check.where: Opening and closing of the DO letter.

rules.title: DO letters are written in the first person
rules.description: A DO letter is written in the first person using an informal conversational style.

rules.title: Abbreviations are normally not used in DO letters
rules.description: Apart from decorations, military symbol identifying references, post office numbers and telephone numbers, abbreviations are normally not used in DO letters.

rules.title: Once used, a common abbreviation must be used consistently
rules.description: Once a common abbreviation has been used in the body of the letter it must be used consistently throughout.

rules.title: Memoranda may use abbreviations throughout
rules.description: A printed memorandum form is designed to save time, is normally written in manuscript, and abbreviations may be used throughout.

rules.title: Email correspondence must still carry reference, date and signature block
rules.description: Email is one of the two types of correspondence and all correspondences must have a file reference, date and signature block.
